utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. I'm sorry that delays with transport of the accused have caused us to have a late start. Good morning, sir. Could I ask you, please, to stand and take the card and read aloud the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Could you state your full name, your profession, and your current position.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Davor Strinovic. I'm a forensic medical expert, a professor at the medical school at the University of Zagreb and deputy head of the institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Could you explain, at the University of Zagreb, what is the nature of your work?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As a professor of forensic science I teach forensic science to medical students, dentistry students, legal students and the police. I also carry out autopsies, and I monitor the work of those specialising in forensic medicine and those students hail from all over Croatia. I also carry out and issue expertise opinions before tribunals. Apart from that, I am engaged in scientific work with a focus on identifying victims of mass disasters and victims of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in December 1991, did you become a member of the Government Commission for Detainees and Missing Persons?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That commission was set up by the Croatian government; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you explain the purpose of that commission?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: The commission was founded in December 1991, primarily because at that time there were large numbers of missing persons and the search for them was to be initiated. We estimated that a portion of the missing persons were still alive and detained somewhere, whereas the others were presumed dead but they were yet to be found and identified. That was the basic role of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you still a member of that commission?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I still am a member of the commission.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And this commission was set up in relation to the effects of the conflict in the former Yugoslavia in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Briefly, what was the nature of the commission's work between 1991 and 1995 whilst the conflict was in process?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Since there were large numbers of missing persons involved, the commission, in its meetings with the other party, that is the representatives of Yugoslavia, to establish as many facts and data concerning the missing people. And to track them in those four years between 1991 and 1995 there were several such meetings, during which we were supposed to discuss the issue of the missing persons and those presumed dead, and those meetings were on a regular basis. Most often in Hungary, in Pecs and Budapest.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Briefly, what was the nature of the cooperation between the Yugoslav government and the Croatian government between that period? Was it smooth or difficult?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: On the one hand, the meetings were quite fair. They were held on a regular basis. We discussed issues, and it was important to keep up the momentum so that both sides would gain the data they needed as to their missing and dead. But as for the results in specific facts and data, those were rather scarce.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: After 1995 did the nature of the commission's work change, and if it did, how did it change?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After 1995, the commission focused mostly on finding mass graves and looking for bodily remains and their identification. But the cooperation continued and is still continuing between Croatia and Serbia on the remaining missing persons who haven't been located as to date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What was your specific role within the commission and what is it now?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, from 1991 until 1995, I was the only forensic member of the commission, and we tried to gather as much data as possible in relation to bodily remains, mass graves, the names and so on and so forth. That was my primary role up until 1995. After that teams were formed for identification in Croatia, and I coordinated their work. Then we began with actual exhumations and identification of those killed during the war. Throughout I coordinated the teams and the tasks all over Croatia, and I took part myself in most of the jobs pertaining to exhumations, identifications, treatment of mortal remains and subsequently identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The exhumations that were conducted as a result of the war in Croatia, were they conducted by the Croatian government, namely through the commission, or were they also conducted by international representatives?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: The exhumations and the process of exhumations was led by the commission for the missing persons of the Republic of Croatia. In some cases the international experts carried out entire procedures; that is, from the exhumation itself up until the identification and determining of elements for identification. In some such instances, international experts came to help the Croatian side. Notably myself acted as monitors in such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So you were the coordinator for the identification of individuals that were exhumed. Were you also the coordinator for the exhumations themselves, the forensic pathologists and other people involved in those exhumations?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you say that you coordinated teams, what types of individuals were in these teams that were involved in the exhumation and identification process? What qualifications did they have generally?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: The part of the teams that I coordinated included a physician, a specialist of either forensic science or a pathologist, and they always had an assistant, a nurse who had had previous experience with exhumations and identifications. That was the medical part of the exhumation team. There were other members of the team, of course, such as necessary to carry out the operation successfully. Sometimes the area had to be de-mined, transportation was needed, but those tasks did not concern any medical staff, and it wasn't under my competence but, rather, the team would usually have a physician and an assistant in its medical component.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In relation to the identification of exhumed bodies, were there other people involved in that process such as dentitions, anthropologists, radiologists, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: The people you mentioned indeed participated in treating or processing the mortal remains. That was the second phase. The first phase is the phase of exhumation. During exhumations, there were entire teams in the field, including the physician and the assistant, and bodies are exhumed, put into bags and then transported to the place to be treated. It was usually done in the field under tents where identification elements were being gathered. And occasionally identifications were carried out as well with the assistance of relatives such as was possible in certain cases when bodies were well-preserved and when we knew we were dealing with small groups of people. In all other cases, a more detailed treatment was necessary because there were more unknown factors. Such cases were treated in various institutes, notably in the forensic institute in Zagreb, but also in Osijek, in Rijeka, in Split and so on and so forth; in larger centres, that is, where forensic medical staff would carry out such determination of elements used for identification and to determine the cause of death. When we had particularly complex cases on our hands and large numbers of dead bodies, such treatment was carried out in Zagreb at the institute for forensic medicine, and we would always bring on board other specialists like a stomatologist, anthropologist, radiologist; that is, the people needed to carry the treatment out as -- in the best way possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. You said anthropologists, radiologists were involved. Can you explain the reason and the importance of the anthropologists being involved in this process and what they can offer in terms of identifying who the individual was?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Anthropologists have their separate role. As time goes by, softer tissues are destroyed and all that is left are bones, skeletons. Proportionately the role of the anthropologist grows with the passing of time. They can read or interpret things other specialists cannot. Therefore, the anthropologist can make his conclusions based on the bones he has at his disposal as to the cause and time of death. That is why anthropologists were important. They could interpret data several years after the actual death as in these cases. In such cases, anthropologists are quite important. They can also establish some basic things such as age, height, then build, as well as potential degenerative changes on the skeleton in terms of pathological health conditions, age, as well as previous trauma of any nature, various anomalies on the bones, fresh, so to say, trauma, and the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said that dental experts were involved in this process. What value do they add to the identification processes? Just briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Dental experts were also important because of the fact that in addition to the bones the only other tissue remaining are actually the teeth. From well-preserved teeth, one can gather much data necessary for identification. Each person is characteristic, having a different set of teeth. An interpretation of a dental expert can provide a lot of elements, based on which in our conversations with the relatives and if we have dental files from before, we can use that to make a positive identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. How does the radiologist assist in the identification process, briefly?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Radiologists are of much help in such identifications because once we begin treating the body, while still in the bag, the radiologist checks it. He looks for any potential metal objects interesting for the process of identification. Braces or anything remaining from previous operations can be used for identification. On the other hand, the radiologist can also detect metal objects that may have been the cause of death. Parts of grenades, shrapnels or other metal objects that could have been the cause of death. Otherwise we wouldn't be able to retrieve them during autopsies because these are small fragments that may have been buried in the bones. But on an X-ray they are well visible. Therefore, they are of much help when determining the cause of death.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. You are currently the deputy head of the Institute of Forensic Medicine in Zagreb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you've been a forensic pathologist for at least the last 26 years; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I concluded my specialisation 25 years ago, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in very brief terms, can you define what forensic pathology is, the nature of that subject matter?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Forensic pathology or, as we call it, forensic medicine, is somewhat different from pathology itself. We deal with violent causes of death, whereas pathology itself deals with disease. Forensic medicine or forensic pathology deals with violent causes of death in -- or, rather, anything that may be useful to a tribunal or a court when determining the cause of death. Therefore, the major difference is the violent factor, to try and determine possible injury or trauma that may have been the cause of death, such as occurs in the cases of homicides, suicides, and so on and so forth. This also includes traffic accidents and all other types of injury, as well as the injuries that may appear during the -- during war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In preparation for your testimony here at the Tribunal in this and other cases, did you prepare an expert report relating to the -- your role in the exhumation and identification process relating to victims in the conflict in Croatia during -- between 1991 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in that report, did you also outline publications in your -- that you have been authors of -- author of and also your professional background?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honours, binders have been distributed with tabs 1 to 7. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Which are just being distributed now. The Defence have received them. They contain a number of documents. At the beginning of that binder there is an index to it and a number of tables that will be referred to in the testimony. The binders have been given to the Defence, and the information has been disclosed. Also Your Honours will receive a chart that was prepared by the witness and brought here yesterday, and that was disclosed to the Defence. And it further explains the identification process.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, if we look at tab number 1 in your binder, do you see the expert report that you've prepared?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: English ERN number 0307-1914 to 0307-1927. And the B/C/S 0117-6675 to 0117-6688. That report, Professor, also contains at the back of the report a number of tables in relation to exhumations conducted in Croatia relating to the conflict. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, those are my tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that report. It's been filed previously on the 15th of September, 2005. And it's registry page numbers 3881 to 3815.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The report will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 451, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, the table, is there to be translation of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, there should be -- there is a translation of the table that relates to the binder itself. There are a number of tables, Your Honour, or charts that are attached to his report which are in English and also translated in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm looking at the separate document that you said arrived yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, this document, it does contain a translation to the extent that hopefully is required. If we look at the top row of the document, we have the English terms immediately above the Croatian terms. And then on the right-hand column we have the translations of the words that appear there when they first appear. Then after that the words repeat themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you are treating it as a self-translating document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And obviously "da" and "ne" are yes and no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That is about the limit of my Croatian, and that is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Because of photocopying, in the centre of the first page of the document at the top I am missing the word above "wounds." Can you tell me what that is?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: It may be "bandages," Your Honour. And -- I believe it may have been "bandages." I'll ask -- perhaps I can ask the witness in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, if you can turn to tab 6 of your binder. And then behind that you have the new document you brought to The Hague. If you look at the column where it states "zavoji ranjavalje," can you translate those words, please?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Bandages. [In English] means bandages, and "ranjavalje" means wounding.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Finally, this table, you are treating as part of Exhibit 451?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that would be separate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you tender it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I tender that table. I can tender that table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit 452, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, looking at your expert report, you refer to a number of publications. Can you briefly describe the number of publications or papers you have written in relation to the identification process of individuals exhumed in a -- wartime situations or in large-scale disasters?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: The one thing I can say is that our first experience at the Zagreb institute was the experience that we had with a large-scale railway accident in 1974 where 200 people were killed. The next page of experience we had was a plane clash over Zagreb with two planes colliding, and there were 170 dead. This was back in 1976. This was a large number of victims that had to be identified. After that, from the beginning of the war in 1991, there were several exhumations. The first was of 20 persons who had been in the country for about six months.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That had been in the ground for 16 months [as interpreted], interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Articles were written to study the various problems normally encountered during exhumations and identification of bodies. We had a five-year project, an American-Croatian project, to identify various dead bodies. This was later carried through by the Croatian ministry. Work continued on identifying dead bodies. Since 1992, there have been a number of international conferences, over 15 I would say, where the research projects were presented as well as the results of our identification efforts. Likewise, two years ago there was a huge conference in Kuwait where identification of bodies in Iraq was discussed. They wanted to hear about our experience in Croatia and I was there as a lecturer to present our experience. I talked about mass graves and exhumations as well as identifying bodies. There is a whole number of conferences. There is a lot of research going on, studying problems of identification, problems related to identifying dead bodies. It was in this way that we have succeeded in amassing a large amount of practical experience and knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how often have you testified in courts of law in relation to forensic pathology opinions, forensic pathologist opinions?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to be specific about the number of opinions, but I offer opinions almost on a daily basis, orally or in a written form. For the last 25 years, I have been giving opinions in writing or orally on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And briefly, the particular nature of your expert opinion, the nature of the testimony?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As a forensic pathologist working at the institute normally I give opinions on general medical issues; murders, traffic incidents. I give opinions on a doctor's responsibility and whatever opinions are requested that have to do with forensic pathology.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you've also testified here at the Tribunal in the Milosevic case in 2003 on the 13th to the 14th of March; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And also in relation to the Martic case in 2006, this year?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you've also testified in the Belgrade trial for the perpetrators for -- the physical perpetrators of the Ovcara incident in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this stage I would seek to tender the testimony in the Milosevic case with ERN numbers 0001-7810 to 0001-7924 from the 13th to the 14th of March, 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I've just been informed there are two separate files, those two ERN numbers, one for the 13th and one for the 14th. But perhaps if it could be one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received as one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 453, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, I'd now like to turn to the actual process of identification. In your expert report you refer to at paragraph 12 two types of processes; one being the classical process of identification, and one being the process by DNA. Can you briefly describe what factors go into identifying someone in the classical method, what you would look for to find a positive identification?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Classical identification means there is a post mortem. When there is a post mortem, an autopsy, elements are gathered that might help towards establishing the identity of a body. You start with the clothes and any items found on the body. Each item, especially jewellery, documents, personal documents and such are very important for identifying the body and as a rule very helpful. The next step is the body itself. The skin can yield a lot of elements useful for identification. Any scars from previous surgery, injuries, old injuries, scar tissue, tattoos, a very typical feature, and where I come from, still very common. This can also be used for identification purposes. The next thing that is important is the teeth. If one is able to study the teeth, this can be used to provide very reliable elements of identification. The teeth remain preserved even if a body spends several years in the ground and that's why they are very useful. They are preserved much better than most of the other organs. The only problem is that in wartime situations medical files were missing and so were dental files. It was difficult to compare what we found with any files, given that most of the files were missing. Furthermore, changes to the bones or to the skull can provide another important element. Every piece of information of that sort, previous trauma, previous surgery, any braces that exist, any scars also provide reliable guide-lines for identifying a body. It is very unlikely that more than one or two people can ever undergo the same kind of surgery in the very same place on the same organ with the same sort of scarring, and this provides more than a reliable hint for identifying a given body. There are a number of elements when talking about classical identification that we look at as forensic pathologists every time we have a new body. When identifying a body, it is especially important to study details, details to do with clothing, with any items found on the body, any peculiarities of the skin, any scar tissue. We hereby derive a whole number of different elements that then we try to piece together to get at a person's identity. Classical identification can only be effective if the so-called antemortem information is gathered at the same time. As soon as a person goes missing we try to get in touch with their families, their nearest and dearest, so that they may provide us with the greatest amount of antemortem information; so to say, pre-death information. We try to get as many useful elements as possible and we then compare anti-mortal information and elements found in the course of an autopsy. We need all of these in order to be able to identify a body. If one uses the classical method and tries to describe all the possible elements, this usually succeeds in about 80 per cent of the cases. I mean of 80 per cent of all the dead bodies subjected to this classical method of identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So in summary, you collect as many identifying features from the body or found on the body itself, and you compare that with information received either before the body was found or after the body was found from relatives, friends, or any other person that may have known that individual?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: It's -- this is probably an obvious question, but how important is it to make sure that the identification that is made, that is finally decided upon, is positive and is a strong identification? And what sort of problems arise in your work if tentative identifications are made incorrectly?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Normally when you start carrying out an autopsy on a body, elements are found that normally provide indications for a possible identification. This is normally termed preliminary identification, which means that you often find a document on a person or some sort of a typical feature, distinctive feature, and this is consistent with some of the antemortem information that we have managed to obtain. Once a body has been processed, a possible identification is established. If there is no sound argument in terms of documents to corroborate this, we then call the family, we tell them about our findings. And then there is also the other element that we normally find strongly indicative, something to suggest that this might be the person, such as personal documents, a case history of their previous illnesses, that sort of thing. So we go through the whole thing with their families. And if a family believes that the elements are not sufficient for a positive ID and we have been unable to establish a sufficient number of elements during our autopsy, then we take further steps. We again reapply the classical method in case there are new elements that emerge, or we may do some DNA analysis. But if there is an identification that has been established but not confirmed by the family, we do not accept this as final. It was for purely practical reasons that we termed this preliminary identification. This was by no means a final identification. If this was not confirmed, it would not be accepted as a final finding, and the body would remain classified as unidentified until final confirmation was obtained. You asked me about the classification. There are several problems that occur here. This is in relation to the elements themselves, how reliable are they, how safe are they, and how much information is obtained from the other side. I'm referring to antemortem information, a-n-t-e, and how much information you can obtain from the family of the deceased. As time goes by, less and less is known about certain things, certain elements. People forget. That is in the very nature of things. So these elements grow more and more meager over the years, and people find it more difficult to be very decided, very determined about certain things. Therefore, we may have an autopsy with a whole lot of information but nothing to compare it to, no one to make a positive ID. And that is when we have no choice but to leave a case open. Sometimes we deal with more subjective problems. Meaning a family, usually the mother, is unable to face the facts. They still keep on hoping that their son is a captive somewhere, still languishing in a prison somewhere but not dead. It is for purely emotional reasons that a mother may be unable to face this sort of reality. This is another aggravating circumstance -- circumstance for the identification process. The simple fact of the matter is unless there is approval from the family, you cannot have a final positive ID. There is maybe one thing I that I would like to point out here. Each case of classical identification must be concluded in a meeting with the family. When they accept the results, they have to sign a statement to that effect. A death certificate is issued to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And to summarise, is it fair to say that in relation to the features attained from the body itself and the antemortem data that you have obtained in relation to the potential identification of that individual, there needs to be a high level of consistency of features pointing to one particular individual before a positive identification is made. Is that a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: That is certainly the essence of what we call the classical method. The important thing is for the pathologist in charge to be as objective as possible. The pathologist must be sure that these are reliable elements, that the elements that he is working with are reliable to have an identification. And then, in a way, he has to be successful in convincing the family, so that they too understand that these are the best, the most reliable results. One thing we have to keep in mind is that those families, those relatives, are not used to images such as those awaiting them in our office. What they see when they come to our office is the remains of a skeleton and not the body, as they remember it. In that situation, a layman may find it hard to accept the appearance of a body like that. This is an experience that is totally alien to them. We have few remains, we have few elements, and yet it is based on this that we wish to build a case for identification, and then we have to get the family to accept this. It is very often difficult to persuade them that this person who was young, who was full of beans, perfectly healthy, is now suddenly dead. There is only a skeleton left and precious little to identify the person. It may be extremely difficult for a family to face the facts, and it may be extremely difficult for us, in turn, to persuade them that this might be the very person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And just briefly, can you explain the process of identification by DNA, in very brief terms, and the reliability of the results?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I do have to point out that I am no DNA expert. I am, however, in touch with the laboratory and with the people who are involved in DNA analysis. This is a new identification method, one that has so far proven to be exceptionally successful. When you have a positive DNA match, that is as good as you can ever get in terms of identifying a body. Each human body has its own DNA, each person has a unique DNA code, so to speak, not shared by anyone else. Only twins can have the same sort of DNA. It is precisely for this reason, because DNA is unique to each person, that the degree of certainty in an identification is practically 100 per cent. When you have DNA analysis, the important thing is to track down the nearest and dearest, the closest possible relative, so that we -- we have DNA samples to compare. What we try to establish is actually paternity or maternity. If there is a missing person and we can track down the mom and dad, we take blood samples for them, and if the -- these samples are confirmed to be consistent, we shall have a near 100 per cent certitude that this is the person because it couldn't possibly be any other person. It is also possible that if a missing person has a wife or a child, we might want to use the same method to achieve the same high degree of certainty in order to prove that this unknown person, this missing person is a child's father. And then this is normally the same kind of percentage that we're looking at, 99.9 per cent of certainty, of certitude. It is also possible in some cases, if there are two or three children, to attain the same high degree of certainty, if this person has fathered two or three children. It is also possible if there is no father, there is just the mother or someone from the mother's family, to use a different method. The first method is the cellular DNA method. This is the most reliable one. There is the mitochondrial DNA method. When you look at the mother's features and her bloodline, the percentages are normally high in terms of certainty, and when identity is established the percentage we normally -- we're normally looking at in these cases is also 99.999 per cent. These methods are extremely reliable methods where you can isolate DNA samples. The problem with bodies that spend a lot of time, a long time in the ground is there is a lot of decomposition, and it is very difficult to isolate DNA samples. But in certain bones, such as the thigh bone, or the teeth, you can still retrieve DNA samples after many years. You can use these samples to compare them to blood samples, the blood samples of close relatives in most cases. There can be a problem, for example, if the body has burnt down; it will obviously be impossible to isolate DNA samples. If a body has been decomposing for a long time, the DNA cells may have disintegrated. This can be due to weather conditions or anything else, but you can have cases where DNA samples may prove impossible to obtain; therefore, you can't have DNA analysis. The problem that we usually face in our work is that there is very often no one to compare this isolated DNA sample to. It's about the nearest and dearest, we can't track these down, these close relatives. Sometimes families leave an area altogether and move elsewhere. We don't have their current address, we have no idea about their whereabouts, so these families don't respond to our summons when we call them to provide blood samples for DNA analysis. These are daily problems that we encounter in our work. Sometimes we have a body, sometimes we have a DNA sample, but there is no way we can establish a person's identify because there's nothing to compare these samples to. We use this as step two, so to speak, as some sort of a back-up option. When our classical procedure fails, we try to do DNA analysis. This has proved to be effective in the great majority of cases, and there is almost -- there is nearly always a positive ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that very complete and comprehensive answer. Dr. Strinovic, I would now like to turn your mind to the exhumation at Ovcara near Vukovar which was conducted in 1996. You were involved in monitoring that exhumation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And now I'd like to take your mind back before that. When did you ever hear of people being evacuated from the Vukovar Hospital and going missing?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was the very next day after it happened. It was on the 20th or possibly the 21st of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Court what you heard in relation to these people going missing from the Vukovar Hospital. You said the very next day. What information did you get and how did you get it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I learned about the missing persons from the Vukovar Hospital via the media. As far as I remember, there were several issues in various papers writing about the missing people and several figures mentioned as well. In any case, a large figure was mentioned of the people who went missing from the Vukovar Hospital on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You stated earlier that the commission was set up in December 1991, the commission for missing persons. Is that correct? The Croatian commission.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When did the -- when did the commission first meet after it was set up?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was in January 1992. We met in Pecs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Where is Pecs, which country?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Pecs is in Hungary, P-e-c-s. It is relatively close to the Croatian border.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the Yugoslav government at that stage, the Serbian government, they had their own commission set up as well in relation to missing persons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did the Croatian commission and the Yugoslav commission, did they meet in Pecs?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Are you able to remember what the subject of discussion was, the main subject of discussion at that first meeting?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was a long time ago. Therefore, my recollection is not so clear anymore. But I know we discussed the missing persons. One of the first questions posed was concerning the missing people from the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: From the Yugoslav government side, from their commission, are you able to remember the individuals or the types of individuals and the positions they held that were representatives of their commission at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I'll do my best. As far as I can remember, the commission was headed by a military person. I believe he was a colonel or lieutenant-colonel by rank. There were representatives of the Yugoslav Red Cross as well, and I can't be any more specific as regards the other people. At the second meeting, I believe, there was a forensic medical specialist from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Between the time that the Ovcara grave was first discovered - and in your Milosevic testimony I think you stated in about October 1992 the grave was first discovered - about how many meetings were held between the two commissions, the Croatian commission and the Yugoslav commission for missing persons, prior to that, prior to that initial discovery of the grave at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I can't be precise. As far as I can remember, in early 1992, from January onwards, we held regular meetings, every month or every 40 days or so. Up until that summer we have had at least four or five meetings in Pecs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned at the first meeting there was a lieutenant-colonel representing -- or as one of the representatives from the Yugoslav commission. Do you mean a lieutenant-colonel from the JNA army at that stage?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about how many representatives did the Croatian side have at these meetings, and who were some of those representatives?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, there was Professor Kostovic on behalf of the Croatian government who was there. Then the lecturer and examiner Mr. Simunovic from the school of law. Then the Red Cross of Croatia. I was there as a forensic pathologist. And that's as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did you attend all of the commission meetings with the Yugoslav government prior to the discovery of the grave? With the commission, I mean.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I attended all of the meetings between January and June 1992. Before the mass grave at Ovcara was discovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And at those meetings how often was the issue of the missing people from Vukovar, how often was that on the agenda at those meetings? At all of them or one of them or ...

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, we discussed it at every meeting. We discussed the people who went missing from the town of Vukovar, with a particular focus on the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And from the representatives of the Yugoslav commission, what was their response to this issue? Did they have any information in relation to them? How did they approach it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As regards the missing people from the Vukovar Hospital, they usually stated that they had no knowledge of such a group and that they could offer no assistance. I think it was what they said, but as I said, it's been a long time ago. That's what I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And about what -- what amount of time was spent in relation to discussing the issue of the missing people from the Vukovar Hospital at these meetings? At the particular meetings.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Such meetings lasted for two or three days, depending on the given meeting. And a large portion of our time was spent discussing the missing people from the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You said that to the best of your recollection you believe that the representatives from the Yugoslav side said that they had no knowledge of such a group going missing. At these meetings with the Croatian commission, did you attempt to persuade the Yugoslav commission that, in fact, people had gone missing? And, if you did, how did you do that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember us discussing that. There were Croatians put by the -- questions put by the Croatian side. By that time we already had some witnesses who could testify as to the missing people from the Vukovar Hospital. We knew they were there, then they went missing. But we also knew of the existence of some lists put together by the physicians or the staff of the hospital and some lists made by the refugees themselves when they came to Zagreb or other parts of Croatia. We knew that a large portion of those people went missing. Some witnesses claimed that they ended up at Ovcara and then we knew nothing of their fate from then on. We don't know whether they were detained or killed. That remained unclear, and we tried to find the truth, but we never did, up until a certain moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And that was information from the witnesses and the lists, et cetera, was that put forward to the Yugoslav commission to assist them in trying to locate these people at these meetings? Either in particular or generally?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As far as I can remember, those meetings were always monitored by various European organisations. We often communicated in English, precisely because of those people who actually chaired those meetings from the international community. As far as I remember, the Croatian side tried to present its arguments or what it knew about the missing people to find out the truth. There are probably records where one could check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And prior to the grave being discovered in October 1992, and apart from the meetings and the discussions that the Croatian commission had with the Yugoslav commission about the missing people, was the fact of missing people from the Vukovar Hospital, was that publicly known prior to the grave being located in October 1992 generally?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there were doubts of the existence of a mass grave, but I can't be any more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we perhaps -- perhaps I will turn to an exhibit now, Your Honour, so perhaps it may be time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will break now and resume at 20 past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, before -- Doctor, before we broke we spoke about the discovery of the grave at Ovcara in 1992. You mentioned that in your testimony in Milosevic, but can you expand on that briefly about when you first heard that the grave site was discovered?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember now, after having discovered the mass grave in October 1992, Dr. Snow came to Zagreb and we heard from him about that. There were also reports in the media. Therefore, I could learn about it in the papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you explain with more detail who Dr. Snow is and what his role was in Croatia at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Dr. Snow is a -- an experienced forensic pathologist who had been invited to Croatia with the intention of trying to locate the mass grave at Ovcara, and so he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did Dr. Snow perform any initial excavation or examination of the Ovcara site when he first arrived at the grave in 1992 or shortly after? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, when he visited Ovcara for the first time when he found an area he thought suspicious, he attempted some excavations. And there were some skeleton remains found in shallow earth, as well as some objects that could have been associated with the persons missing from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Have you seen any photographs of that initial examination of the site by Dr. Snow?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have, but later.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when did you first see those photographs in relation to that examination at the site?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm uncertain whether that was in 1996 when Snow returned to Croatia or whether it was here at this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And 1996 was when the full exhumation of the site occurred?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know why the site wasn't exhumed or the bodies weren't exhumed in 1992, when it was discovered, and four years had passed before the exhumation was fully undertaken?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the exhumation could not have been carried out back in 1992 because the local Serbs wouldn't permit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know why they didn't allow the exhumation to occur then?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I can only presume or guess at their reasons. I guess they were afraid of others finding this -- finding out about this horrible truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say "the local Serbs," are you referring to just local civilian people, or are you referring to the local Serb government at the time? Who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I had in mind all of them whom you mentioned now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If we can go to -- it's not the exhibit that I referred the ushers to beforehand, but if we can go to 65 ter video, which is 316, and we can play it on Sanction. There is a series of photographs that relate to the initial discovery of the site, and I would ask that you see those photographs and then comment on them at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could stop the video there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Looking at this slide, I believe it's slide 5, what is that a picture of?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: On slide 5 we see an aerial photograph. Next to the forest to the right side of the photograph there is a depression which didn't look natural. That was one of the reasons that they attempted to find or locate a mass grave there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If we can continue with the slides.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If we can stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I believe this is slide 15. Doctor, can you explain what is occurring in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Before I do that, I wanted to say that we saw a sequence of photographs. Some of them were obviously taken in October, and we see the vegetation that is green at that time. That was the first visit of Dr. Snow. He came across an area, a depression, and next to a forest. Then they became suspicious that that could be the location of the grave. He found the skeleton, including the skull you could see in shallow ground. And in terms of indicators, that sufficed to become suspicious of the existence of the grave. Some of the other photographs may have been made later in December when he returned and they did initial or testing excavations in order to be able to approach the bodies to try and determine the actual size of the mass grave. That's why we see this ditch here. In order to try and approach the bodies to determine the size of the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If we can move to the next slides, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If we can stop the slide there, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I believe this was slide 21. The person that we see in the photograph, is that Mr. Snow, or Dr. Snow?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is Dr. Snow. There is no mistake because he used to wear that hat all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can you describe what he's doing in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Dr. Snow approached the skeletal remains, and he is measuring the femur here to determine the height and possibly the age of that person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If we can move to the next slides, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Doctor, looking at those slides, briefly can you describe the process that occurred in that first excavation of Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: The initial exhumation was begun in October with the first of Dr. Snow's visits when he discovered the suspicious area next to the forest. He also was able to establish that there were bones protruding out of the earth and he established them as being human bones and a skull of a young male. There were also some objects next to the bone, and he could safely assume that it was a person of Croatian ethnicity, because of the symbols they represented, being the cross and a rosary, as well as a picture of a saint. And on the second occasion, when exhumations were carried out, they were more detailed and precise. They tried to measure the size of the mass grave and the position of the bodies, as well as to try and assess the number of bodies. That's why they tried digging out small, shallow trenches, or corridors, so to speak, to try and determine the limits of the grave. Those were all testing or initial exhumations by which they sought to confirm that indeed it was a mass grave, and that more than one body could be found there. This being confirmed, as far as I remember, they put the earth back, they marked the limits of the mass grave, and put under guard by the UN soldiers up until the moment of true exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And so the remains were placed back in the grave and then the dirt was covered over? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that video. It was tendered in the Dokmanovic case through Dr. Clyde Snow, and it's 65 ter number 316.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The slides will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 454, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I would now ask that we move to 65 ter number 974. It's a newspaper article dated the 28th of October, 1992. It's a newspaper article from Novi Vjesnik. Your Honours, at this stage the translation is being prepared, and so unless -- if there is any objections to tendering, we can have the translation -- have the article marked and then the translation admitted hopefully in the next couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, if we can look at -- firstly could you read the title of the article?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: "Are there any living beings in the darkness at Ovcara."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if I could ask --

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Or, "Is there anyone still alive in the darkness of Ovcara."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I could ask the registry representative if she could enlarge the right-hand side of the article, that boxed -- thank you, that boxed section. And perhaps one size larger, so that Dr. Strinovic can read it. Just that first paragraph, thank you. Dr. Strinovic, could you read that first paragraph, the title and read the first paragraph, and then I'll ask you a couple of questions about that, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: "Is the grave concealing the wounded from the hospital? The discovery of a mass grave near Vukovar in the report of Tado Samasivjeski [phoen], the plenipotentiary of the UN Commissioner for Human Rights in the former Yugoslavia, has this day shaken both the domestic public and the international public as well as a great number of people from Vukovar, who are still hoping for one of the next exchanges where they might finally get to meet some of their near relatives. Additional disquiet was caused by the statement of Clyde Snow, forensic pathologist and a member of the UN Commission for Human Rights for investigating crimes in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, who in an interview to the American journalists on Monday evening disclosed that the mass grave found with bones protruding actually contained bodies from the 174 Croats detained at the Vukovar Hospital who were first tortured and then killed. He also invokes witness statements that were used to locate the protruding bones. It is for this reason that we have decided to interview Vesna Bosanac, the once director of the Vukovar Hospital, and today's health minister, Dr. Jure Njavro, who were eyewitnesses to the war horrors of Vukovar."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can move to the second page, please. And to the bottom right-hand side. Thank you. Just showing the newspaper and the date right at the footer of the page, please. If we can just go down further. Thank you. Thank you. Doctor, the -- this paper is Novi Vjesnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And it's dated the 28th of October, 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And Novi Vjesnik, is that a Croatian paper?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender that document, which is 65 ter number 974. And would be providing a translation in the next couple of days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 455, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, you stated that the exhumation wasn't carried through because the local Serb authorities did not allow that to occur. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And between 1992 and the full exhumation in 1996, was that site that was found by Dr. Snow, was that protected, security-wise?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, yes. Throughout that period there was someone guarding the site, UN troops guarding the access to the site and the grave itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So the best of your knowledge, between the time that it was discovered and the time that the full exhumation commenced, the grave site wasn't interfered with?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then when in 1996 did the full exhumation occur?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, this happened on the 31st of August. Well, actually, information started leaking through, if you like, throughout September and October 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And that exhumation, to your knowledge, was conducted under the authority -- the Tribunal -- Tribunal's authority, the Yugoslav Tribunal's authority; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that, too, is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How long did the exhumation last, retrieving the bodies from the grave, and then delivering them to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: The procedure itself took about two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: After the bodies were transferred to Zagreb, were autopsies conducted on each and every one of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the bodies were brought to the forensic pathology institute, international pathologists and domestic pathologists examined every single body.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were those autopsies done in 1996, at the end of 1996?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That, too, is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who actually carried out the exhumation and the autopsies?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: The exhumation, as well as the autopsies, were conducted by international experts. The whole process was monitored by the Croatian side, myself and other colleagues who would occasionally stand in for me. And this applied to both the exhumation itself and the autopsies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And were representatives from the Yugoslav government, were they present at the exhumation and the autopsies?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: That is also true. From the time the exhumation began and throughout the autopsies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So in relation to the exhumation and the autopsies, your role as the forensic pathologist within the commission set up for locating missing persons, that was to monitor rather than to conduct the exhumation or autopsies?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: That is also absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And after the autopsies were completed, is it the case that the Croatian commission for missing persons had the responsibility of carrying out the identification process and not the Tribunal or the international experts?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: That is true in its entirety. The moment the autopsies were concluded, the Croatian side obtained everything that was pertinent to the identification process and we started the procedure right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you present at the exhumation in 1996 and, if you were, for about how many days were you present there?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I would occasionally attend the exhumation. From the start to the end I came about 10 times myself, and the rest of the times a colleague who normally attended the exhumation would go there to replace me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to show you a series of photographs taken from the exhumation in 1996, and I would ask if you could comment on them. Photographs, 65 ter number 878. Doctor, looking at photograph 1, can you explain what we see there? Just briefly.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: This is the site of the mass grave. In this photograph, you can see a depression, the ground is depressed, and the landscape has been altered. It is not consistent with the landscape all around this site. There had obviously been alterations made to this site, and that's why suspicions arose that this might be the site of a mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the fence that we see on photograph 1, is that -- was that erected to protect the site?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. That's why the fence is there. Wasn't always there. It was put up because of the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could turn to photograph 2, please. The white building that we see in photograph 2, what is that building, Doctor? On the right-hand side; it's a little bit hard to see, but ...

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, this was a section of the building that was added later on. This was a facility where the experts were accommodated, and they carried out some of their preparations in that building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can slowly click through from 3 to 4, and then stop at 5, please. Thank you. Doctor, looking at photograph 5, what do we see here?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: We see a new road here for the purposes of the exhumation. We see a fence that protected the grave site and the experts in order to shield the whole procedure from view, as it were. In order to keep anyone on the outside looking inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And again, if we could move slowly through from 6 to 10, and then stop at 10, please. Doctor, looking at slide 10, is this a trench that is being dug to commence the exhumation?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: This was the real start of the exhumation. The outer limits of the grave were marked, and then they started with this so that they could approach the bodies and determine the size of the grave itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can move through slowly to 12 and stop at 12, please. And, Doctor, looking at this plastic sheeting that we see, what's the purpose of that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: When a day's work was finished, at night the plastic sheeting that you can see here would be spread across the grave to keep it from the elements, from rain, until a tent was eventually put up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can move through to 14, please. Doctor, looking at the excavator that we see in the photograph, what -- how did that assist in the exhumation, and how was that used?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: This was a large area, a large grave. In order to be able to approach the bodies, in order to arrange the earth around the grave itself, one needed an excavator to carry out these preparations so that one might then start excavating by hand, as it were, as soon as one got close enough to the actual bodies in the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can move to 15, please. If we could enlarge it one level. Thanks. Doctor, looking at this photograph here, in the foreground of the photograph, what do you see?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: There are visual hints here, these seem like bones, but the photograph is not exactly crystal clear, so it's a bit difficult for me to comment on this particular photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps if we move through to 16. This photograph, can you explain what we see here?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Another aerial photograph of the fenced-off area around the mass grave, and the grove itself, which is just adjacent to the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If we can move to 17, please. Doctor, just above the pencil in that photograph, what do you see?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: You can see a bullet, a fire-arm bullet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If we can move slowly through to 19, please. And if we can enlarge one size. Thank you. And perhaps even one size again. Thanks. Doctor, looking at this photograph, what do you see here?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: In this photograph, we can see around the edges of the photograph a trench all around the grave. The exhumation of bodies has begun. You see intertwined bodies in the foreground, and to the left you can see that this is indeed a mass grave, that there is a whole mass of bodies there lying intertwined and strewn around.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Slide 20, please. Doctor, looking at this scaffolding, or beginnings of a building, can you explain why this was erected?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Autumn was on its way, and the autumn rains were too. The ground was wet, so this was done in order to avoid problems with the rain. This plastic sheeting was used at first, but then the idea occurred to someone to put up a rather large tent in order to protect the entire site and in order to improve the working conditions during the actual exhumation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could move through to slide 23, please. And perhaps if we can enlarge that to one more level. Thank you. Doctor, in slide 23, what do you see there?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I think this is a photograph of a lot of bodies lying there intertwined. That is how the photograph was taken before the digging began where the bodies were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And slide 24, please. Doctor, looking at this photograph, can you explain what you see, and can you also indicate what the meaning of that number 5 is?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: In this photograph you can see a number of bodies, and then one particular body is shown. You can see the legs, you can see the trunk, the rump, and you can see the head. The number 5 here, I suppose, must be in reference to case number 5, the Ovcara case. When bodies were extracted, it was done on individual basis, one by one, and then number 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and all the way up to 200. I suppose the number 5 tag attached to this body means that this was the fifth body extracted or pulled out of the mass grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And those numbers that were assigned to the bodies that were in the grave, did those numbers stay with the bodies right through the completion of the exhumation process, the autopsy process, and the identification process? And does that appear in all of the records that you have at the commission today?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: That is most certainly true. A lot of attention was paid to this, to keeping the chronological order intact, to keep the numbers the same all the time. Once the numbers were mixed up, identification would become more difficult. But the numbers were always the same from the time a given body was exhumed until a positive ID was finally made. And the numbers are still the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: On that point, you stated that you didn't conduct an exhumation yourself but you monitored it. What was your assessment of the work that was done by the pathologists that were involved in the exhumations in relation to how carefully they carried out the exhumation?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Those were, for the most part, archaeologists who carried out all the necessary preparations and who did the digging itself. This was done by experts in archaeology and that was done in a very neat and impeccable way, you must say, and I have no objections to their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can move slowly through to slide number 28, please. Doctor, looking at slide 28, can you explain what you see in this photograph? What is happening at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: In this photograph you can see the following: Once the grave was dug up in its entirety and all the bodies were in a single mound, the bodies were carefully extricated with all the clothing, wherever there was some, and the bodies were placed in white bags; you can see the white bags in the photograph. There would be a plastic number attached to the body itself, and then the same number would be put on the bag, 1 to 200. So this was a preliminary step before the bodies were eventually taken to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can just go back to slide 25, I think. Perhaps slide 26. Thank you. Doctor, looking at the photograph here, can you explain what you see?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: In this photograph I can see an open grave, I can see the bodies inside, a mound of bodies all thrown together. It's a huge grave with a lot of bodies. The bodies are about to be placed in the white bags. You can see some stretchers along the edge, and those were used to take the bodies to the containers before further processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And approximately what size was the grave, in terms of the size of the pile of the bodies?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I know someone did get the dimensions, the size. In my estimate, it could have been 15 or 20 metres across.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you mentioned earlier that there were 200 bodies found at this grave site. We can -- we will discuss the figures a little more shortly. But is that the correct number of bodies that were found at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were exactly 200 bodies found at Ovcara.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can move to slide 29, please. Doctor, can you explain what you see here and the relevance of this photograph?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: It was a large grave with many bodies, some of which are closer to the surface. In some of the initial photographs during testing excavations we saw some parts of the skeletons and bones that were skeletonised. The bodies that were deeper in the ground, some parts of skin were also preserved, among other elements necessary for identification. In this photograph, we see a piece of skin with a tattoo, which is quite specific and recognisable. Using such an identification element, we can safely identify the person. Unfortunately, there weren't so many cases of skin with tattoos, but in cases there were such elements the process of identification was being far easier -- was being made far easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And that number, 190, relates to the number that was assigned to that individual throughout this whole process; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. As I stated before, the particular number for the particular body throughout the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can move through to photograph 31. Thank you. And, Doctor, looking at photograph 31, can you explain briefly what you see there?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: On this photograph we see the white bags, one of which is open. There was a body put inside, and the bag was to be closed off, and there is a number inside the bag and on the outside of the bag. And in such way the bodies were transported onwards to the forensic institute for further processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can move through to photo 35, please. Now, Doctor, looking at photograph 35, what is occurring or what has occurred just recently before this photograph was taken?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: This photograph was taken at the end of the exhumation when the entire grave had been emptied. The bodies were put in plastic bags and taken away. This is what was left behind. That's the empty mass grave, which was then again covered with earth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender those photographs, and they're photographs in 65 ter 878.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 456, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Dr. Strinovic, you stated that after the -- well, firstly, the 200 bodies that were found at Ovcara, were they taken back to the forensic institute in Zagreb, where you worked?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. The bodies were transferred to the forensic institute in Zagreb, and that's where the international experts carried out the autopsies of all the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you stated earlier that you weren't responsible for carrying out the autopsies, but you monitored how those autopsies were carried out. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You have stated your opinion as to how the exhumation was carried out. In relation to the autopsies, what is your opinion in how those pathologists carried out their work?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: In principle I have no objections. They did their part of the work very well, though some details made things a bit more difficult for us later on when trying to identify, because perhaps they offered too little detail and photographs that subsequently proved important for identification. Therefore, we needed a bit more time to see things through. But generally speaking, everything was done according to the rules of their profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then in 1997 those, the bodies that were discovered at Ovcara, they were handed over into -- they were placed into your custody or the forensic institute's custody, or more broadly, the commission for missing persons custody, is that correct, to carry out the positive identifications?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So the responsibility of the internationals was simply to try and determine the cause of death?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: That was their primary task. Since they carried out the autopsies in a proper way, they described everything else that may not have been linked directly to the cause of death, but was linked to the process of identification. Therefore, we received their documentation making it far easier for us to carry out identifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And is it correct that one aspect of their documentation that you did not receive was the information relating to the cause of death, as opposed to identification information?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct as well. We received all data necessary for identification, and we were told that we can get the data relating to the humanitarian issue of identification. As for the actual cause of death, we were told that this was within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal and that we may not -- we couldn't be provided with such documentation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can ask you to turn to tab 4 of our -- of your binder and our binders, please. And this is a table entitled "Paragraph 49." And the ERN number 0327-2129. And it relates to a chart that was prepared for the Milosevic case and which was tendered through you in that trial. When we look at this chart, do you know who prepared this table?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The table was prepared at our institute. I did that with the assistance of my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
