utterances.text: And does this table relate to certain statistics relating to cause of death, and also some broad identifying features of the 200 bodies that were exhumed at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. One can clearly see that from the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if we look at the table, in relation to causes of death, that information you stated wasn't initially given to you when you were doing the identifications. However, did you subsequently receive information as to the individual causes of death relating to the bodies from some source?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The data on the causes of death was received subsequently. I don't know exactly when, but it could have been sometime in 2002 or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in that table the cause, how many -- firstly, how many cases was the cause of death established? Perhaps it's obvious, it was in 195 cases. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. We can see that from the first column where the cause is established, that the number is 195.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And how many individuals were killed as a result of shooting?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: [In English] 188. [Interpretation] 188.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in relation to the causes of death in relation to trauma, we have six individuals, and other violence we have one. Does that mean that those individuals were not shot, or is it an equivocal figure in relation to shooting? What do those figures mean?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to provide a precise comment on these figures, but if trauma is mentioned as the cause of death instead of shooting, one would expect that that body did not sustain an injury from a fire-arm, but rather from -- by another source. Some sort of force was applied, perhaps it could have been strangulation or something else. But I can't really provide any comment without going into the documentation itself. As regards your question, according to the data we have and on the basis on which the data was compiled, out of 188, those people were shot, six had trauma excluding fire-arm woundings as the cause of death, and the same goes for that one case of other violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Is it possible that someone could be shot but that not be shown up in a cause of death on an autopsy report? Is that a possibility?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Of course it is. Especially in cases when we have bodies which spent several years under the ground and the soft tissue disintegrated. For example, if one received a bullet through the heart, the soft tissues are gone and there are no injuries to the bones. It is possible to sustain such a wound. During an autopsy, we wouldn't be able to ascertain the cause of death. We can't establish that that person was shot, although he or she could have been. Therefore, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, I'm about to ask you some questions about the -- some of the identifying statistics in relation to these bodies that were find.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: But, Your Honours, it's 12.30. I wonder if lunch is at 12.30 or 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Lunch is at 12.30. Are you tendering this table?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but I have a few extra questions in relation to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it now, so that the record discloses that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 457, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We resume at 1.45. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.32 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Judge Parker is unable to sit this afternoon, so pursuant to the Rules, Judge Thelin and myself will be sitting alone. Mr. Smith, before you start, we would like to indicate to you that we would suggest to have the break at 3.00 so that the afternoon session is better cut into two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: All right. I'll take that into account. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Doctor, before the break we were referring to Exhibit 457, and this was the chart that your office prepared in relation to the cause of death and some identifying features of the bodies that were exhumed from Ovcara. I would now like to ask you to explain briefly the comment in this chart that 86 of -- were previously wounded and 114 were not previously wounded. Can you explain what that means, "previously wounded"?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: This concerns some people from the hospital, and it was to be expected that some of those were -- had been wounded before or had been sick, and therefore admitted into the hospital. What we were able to conclude, based on the information we received, and we could see there information on wounds and previous injuries, and it was stated there that those wounds or injuries must have been the reason for their admittance to the hospital. This concerns 86 people. The international experts, in carrying out their autopsies, found evidence of previous wounds. As for the other 114, there were no entries made regarding their possible wounds sustained before, and those people had no visible trauma that may have been there before they were admitted to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What was the average age of the individuals that were killed at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: After the process of identification was carried out we could be precise as to the average age, which was, according to our data, 32.5 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in the -- in your statistics you state that there were 198 males, that were exhumed, and two of them were female. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. As can be seen in the paragraph 49 table before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the age -- the age range of those individuals exhumed, what was that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: According to the data and identification, we could see the age average of the bodies treated, and that was between 16 and 72.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can now move to tab 3, that previous document has been tendered already. Tab 3 of your binder. And this chart is entitled "Summary of examination findings." Do you have that table in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the ERN number is 0327-2169 to 0327-2176. Who prepared this table?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, this table was prepared by the international experts who carried out the identifications. According to the data from the table, we could see it was prepared on the 12th of June, 1997. I think it was a mistake though. I think it should have been 97 instead of 07; therefore, in 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And briefly could you explain what this table shows. If we can go from left to right and explain the criteria that's listed in this table, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: On the table first we have case numbers or Ovcara numbers, as we call them. The way -- or in the sequence the bodies were exhumed from 1 to 200. So we started with case number 1, of course. Then date. I believe it to be the date of exhumation. Or rather, the initiation of examination. Then age. Sorry, first gender, then age, age in terms of the minimum and maximum number of years. That means together with the dental expert and the forensic pathologist, the anthropologist is attempting to assess the age of the person based on the remains treated during the abduction [as interpreted] giving the minimum and maximum number of years and then the mean values being calculated. Then height, minimum and maximum, of course. We -- since we couldn't measure bodies in full, we used separate bones, and in our calculations we receive the possible range of height and then we calculated the mean, the mean value. After that there is death, the cause of death with a description of cause as well as manner, meaning homicide. And the last column is tentative identification. In those cases in which, based on certain elements, the experts thought that a name could be ascribed to a particular body, and all effort was made to reach the proper -- the conclusion about the identity of the person. Once we had all the elements necessary, we could perhaps make a positive identification out of the 200 that were found there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to tentative identifications of these individuals that were exhumed, of the 200 about how many were tentatively identified by the internationals that were doing the autopsies, from that chart? Are you able to say?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: If you take all the tentative identification cases we come up with a total of 56.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you said earlier that your responsibility was to ensure -- or the commission's responsibility was to ensure that the bodies were identified correctly, and the internationals' responsibility, the ones that carried out the autopsies, was to establish the cause of death. Did you accept these tentative identifications as final identifications, or was more work done to ensure that people were identified correctly?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: In the cases where the so-called preliminary or probable identification existed, during our process of identification we ran checks on that, meaning that we tried to compare that with the antemortem data that we have been collecting as of the moment those people went missing. We had a database in place for all those missing in Croatia, including the area of Vukovar and its hospital. Once in possession of such data, we could cross-reference that with other information that we received from the family and friends and compare that with the findings of the autopsies, in cases of persons for whom tentative identification was attempted. Then we had more elements in place, based on the additional information received. That's how we tried to verify things. And when we thought there were sufficient elements in place to make an identification, in the cases of tentative identification we tried to get in touch with their families. We would tell their families why we called them; that is, that we were being -- we thought that we may have one of their family members at the institute, and then they would be asked to come and make a positive identification or not. In the case of Ovcara, these tentative or preliminary identifications were carried out first. Out of the 200 John Does, we had a number of people for whom we may have been in possession of their names. Once accepted by their family, we could be certain that we have a positive identification, and then the bodies were turned over to their families and properly buried, concluding the process of identification after the family has signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Can you explain why your office, the commission for missing persons, and in particular your role in the forensic institute, was to -- why your office was chosen to identify these people in a positive manner as opposed to the internationals that were conducting the autopsies? Why weren't they given that responsibility?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: It is difficult to give you a precise answer, but I may offer my opinion. The international experts were in charge of the exhumations up to the point of autopsies and determining the cause of death. That was the primary task of those experts. Such data was then forwarded to the Tribunal as to the cause of death. When one is treating bodily remains, we also need to involve identification elements. In their work they gathered a number of such elements, they would note them down on paper, and then they forwarded that to us to continue with the humanitarian part of the operation as regards identifications. The basic task of those experts was to carry out autopsies, to come up with the number of the victims, as well as to establish the cause of death. The latter portion of the process was left to the Croatian side to follow through. Since the entire treatment was done at the forensic institute, where we had the best conditions, we had all the equipment necessary, including the X-ray machines and separate halls to carry out identifications. And being the leading such an institution in Croatia, such cases were treated in Zagreb, and that's why the institute was tasked with the second part of the process to carry out the identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And on this table we can also see what I believe to be the anthropologist involved in the autopsy, as well as the pathologist; is that correct? Or does the anthropologist relate to the exhumation itself? And I'm referring to the third column, and I think it's about the 9th or 10th column, for the anthropologist -- I mean pathologist?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I think we're talking about A-n-t-h, the heading A-n-t-h, is that what you're referring to? That's it, yes. I think we have the names of the pathologists here. Their initials. They were involved with processing information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in relation to the third column where we have A-n-t-h, is that short for anthropologist, or does that relate to the pathologist as well?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that the third one is in relation to the anthropologists. And the next one, P-a-t-h, is probably the pathologists. That's my assumption. We had both kinds of experts on these international teams. The final finding would be a joint one. It was normally an autopsy report that was important for ascertaining the cause of death and for subsequent identification. The Croatian side was eventually only given details as they related to the identification procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender that document. 0327-2169 to 2176.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 458, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, Doctor, if we can turn to tab 5, please, of your binder, and of our binders. And this is ERN number 0327-2177 to 0327-2182. And it's a list of names. Can you explain to us -- well, firstly, who prepared this table; do you know?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, this table was produced by the Croatian commission for detained and missing persons. We see the names of those identified, their date of birth, and the status of their identification. At the end of that table we have a list of missing persons who were not identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And this table was tendered through you in the Milosevic case in 2003. Are you able to say whether this table was accurate at the time that you tendered it in the Milosevic case, in terms of people that have been identified who were found in the grave at Ovcara?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: All the information in this table was obtained from the forensic pathology institute where the identification procedure was carried out. All the names should be consistent with the original document. The list should be consistent with the persons who were identified. This is in actual fact information originating from our institute, once the identification procedure had been dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Of the 200 Ovcara victims that were found in the grave, on my count there are 11 victims who -- who names -- who hadn't been identified as of 2003, is that correct, from this table.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, in the column on the right-hand side we have status, and it has, I believe, positive identification; that's a short form is written there, Pos. Id. Is that quite a different form of identification to the identification we looked at that was provided by the internationals at the autopsies in 1997 when it was listed as tentative identification?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: That's right. As I've explained before, preliminary identification does not constitute a final identification. It's just a way to make the job easier on those who are carrying out the final evaluation of all the data obtained. They have the names to go on and they can then speed up the identification process. Preliminary identification is just an initial stage. What we have in front of us, the document, contains positive IDs, which means their families accepted the results and then these are the final designations, as it were, given to the bodies identified, their names and numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I seek to tender this -- I seek to tender this document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit 459, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Doctor, if we can now turn to tab 6, please, of the binder. And this is a list of -- a list of names with what appears to be the method of identification on the right-hand side, whether it was via classical or DNA methods. And the ERN number is English 0469-8425 to 0469-8429, and the B/C/S 0469-8425 to 0469 -- sorry, that's my mistake there. The B/C/S is 0469-8425 -- perhaps it wasn't, 8427. Do you see that document in front of you, Doctor?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who prepared this document?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: This one was prepared by our institute of forensic pathology, which means that it was produced by my colleagues and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if we look at the end of the document, it states there are a total of 200 persons where eight were unidentified. This document was prepared this year; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: So between 2003 and 2006 there were a further three people, that were previously unidentified, identified; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Which leaves, of the 200 people, exhumed from Ovcara, eight still unidentified?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Right again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Why is it so difficult to identify, say, these last eight bodies? Just briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As I've pointed out in my introduction concerning identification problems, it is obvious that in these cases we weren't able to contact any relatives to confirm our DNA identification. In these cases the classical method is out of the question, since there are too few elements to go on in order to solve these cases. That's why we used DNA analysis to isolate these eight remaining cases. The thing is, we couldn't get through to their relatives in order to obtain blood samples to use for a comparison. We don't know which list these eight persons belonged to. It could be a larger number of persons or a smaller number of persons. I'm talking about who these eight bodies might be. Why do we not have a blood sample? There are several possibilities. There may be no relatives around or alive. It might also be the case that their family had, at some point, moved, relocated and we had no means of contacting them. And this was not only a problem with Ovcara. This also applied to a number of other situations. We have currently in Zagreb about 500 bodies waiting identification. The classical method has been applied, DNA samples were extracted from their bones and teeth, but we are still unable to trace these people back to any specific names. So the same would seem to apply to this large number of bodies that we've processed, about 4.000 persons. As to these eight unidentified bodies from Ovcara, we are unable to establish identity simply because we do not have the sort of blood samples necessary to confirm the identity of those bodies. This situation might be expected in a disaster such as war. It's very difficult to track down relatives. It's very difficult to obtain blood samples to use in order to confirm the identity of these bodies. We shall be forging ahead, we shall further pursue this and try to get to these blood samples, but as time goes by I think this might prove to become increasingly difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And I notice at the end of the chart you state that: "Of the 192 identified, 93 were identified in the classical manner and 99 by DNA."

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Of the 192 people that have been identified, are you able to say what ethnicity these people were?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: We don't have that indicated in these tables. I can only say that the great majority of these persons are Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say the "great majority," can you put an approximate figure, a statistical figure on that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: 95 per cent, 98 per cent, perhaps more. One would need to go back to the table, one would need to retrieve this particular piece of information, because it is there, it is available. If you would like to have another table with the ethnicity stated, I think that would be possible. The percentage, at any rate, of Croats would be exceedingly high.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, were you able to compare the spellings of some of these names in the 2006 list, the one that your office prepared, to the list that was produced by the internationals in 1997, and in some cases did you notice a few spelling differences between the names, slight variations?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did check that, as a matter of fact. And I ascertained that in some cases, not too many though, there have been spelling discrepancies, as it were. Which is only understandable, if you bear in mind who carried out the identification procedures and who wrote these names. It is possible that the international experts may have left out a letter or two, and that is why errors occurred. This is only understandable, given the nature of the work performed and given the complexity level of some of the names being mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When comparing this 2006 list to the 1997 list, there are two tentative identifications which are different to the positive identifications in your list. And firstly, I refer to individual number 50 on your list, the 2006 list, where in 2006 you have that no one has been identified at this stage. Is that correct? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. I can explain that, briefly. Preliminary identification does not amount to final identification, as I've pointed out before. It does indicate who the person might be, it does give us a lead, as it were, but this, as a rule, needs further confirmation, further elements before it can be set in stone, as it were. As an expert, I do understand why this must be this way. This is not to detract from the value of preliminary identification. Oftentimes it is proved to be accurate. But it is nothing more than just that, and it can only be expected that cases may occur where identification is not confirmed, which again I must say, is perfectly understandable under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And would this apply also to individual 146, who is identified in your chart has Damir Simunic, but was tentatively identified as Marko Ribic? Does that same answer apply to that difference?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly, the same answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit 460, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Doctor, if we can now go to Exhibit 452, which was the chart that is not in the binders but was given to counsel and Your Honours separately. This is the chart that's headed "classic," and it has a number of identifying factors that enabled your office to form a positive identification. Do you have that document in front of you? It's ERN number 0600-3011?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And perhaps rather than me explain the chart, if you can explain the chart and the purpose of it.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: This chart or table shows cases of classical identification. You have the numbers of the so-called Ovcara cases, and the names of those identified. And then you have the most usual elements used in identifying a body. Each piece of information is important for a possible identification. The more elements, the more reliable an identification, and the easier it is to track down a body's family, so to speak. We're talking about the classical method. We have those who are younger and those who are older, and then we can introduce subsets in order to arrive at a final identification. Then we have the question of teeth; we've spoken about that. Teeth are always a peculiar feature of any body. If there is a good deal of reliable antemortem information, if there are dental files, then this is very helpful in identifying a body. These are the most important primary signs that go towards establishing a body's identity. Depending on where a body was found, and I'm talking about Ovcara, whether it was on the surface, in those cases sometimes only skeletons remained, but if bodies were buried deeper in the ground, then very often the skin too was preserved, as well as hair, which was used in some of the cases. That was another element to help identify a body. And there are special features, what we describe as special features, possible anomalies, previous changes to the tissues, something that might help us with identification. Whenever there were indications, this was something that we could use, since most of these anomalies are not something that everybody has, but rather very few people. These are normally unique and as such very helpful. The next column, bandages and wounds, we are looking at people who were at some point hospitalised. If their skin was preserved, you could see if there were had been any previous injuries or fractures, not necessarily causing death but previous fractures and injuries. On the other hand, you have bandages and you have plaster-casts, limbs being immobilised, the normal sort of assistance administered in a hospital. You have a patient with a plaster-cast or with a bandage on their arms or legs. Now, this is normally something that can also prove very helpful in identifying a body. In a number of such cases where we did, in fact, have antemortem information on a person, we had some of their case histories, when they were hospitalised, why, where, what exactly did they, have plaster-casts, bandages, was the wound seen to surgically and so on and so forth. So this was the sort of information that we found very helpful in our work, and this proved to be just that, very helpful. These were solid elements that we could rely on for identification. Items of clothing, that was helpful to too, needless to say. When and where it was relatively well preserved. Especially if relatives could be tracked down, who were perhaps familiar with a particular item of clothing. Something that is normally invisible to an untrained eye, so to speak. Some of the relatives may have made those clothes or patched them up or whatever. Only the person who did this would be in a position to know, and this is very convincing proof, because whenever this was the case this was a solid foundation for identifying a body. For example, a mother may know that she at one point in time mended the shirt of her son. She knows precisely what sort of a patch she put there. If you can produce that item of clothing, if you can show her, she may be in a position to say positively, yes, this is something I did, or perhaps I never did this, but that is why clothing can sometimes be very important for identification. And if this occurs, the mother is likely to accept identification because she is then convinced and absolutely certain that she was the one who did that. She finds it easier to accept the identification of her son's dead body. Documents, this is not only ID, this is not only about passports, it's also a reference to other documents, such as case histories, a doctor's referral, that sort of thing. This is not very often the case, but whenever these are found, then if you have a document like that, you can categorise the person as a possible ID, and this makes it easier to eventually identify that person. Obviously if you see somebody's ID in somebody's pocket, it is quite clear that is something that the family are more likely to accept as such. Because this is very palpable, it's tangible, it's incontrovertible very evidence, you might say. The next category is jewellery. When found, this can be extremely valuable, because again jewellery is something that is usually unique. If you have the wedding ring, there's usually the name engraved right there, sometimes a date, a distinctive feature in one word. If we're talking about other types of jewellery, there can be all different kinds, colour, shape, make, you can even trace it back to a particular goldsmith at times. This may all be very relevant. For example, if you have a wedding ring bearing the year, name and date, this is very strong proof, it's material evidence, and it might prove relatively easy to identify that person, having found that items or identifying objects, a whole range of items found on a body such as keys, other types of items. A comb, a lighter, that sort of thing. This may also be very interesting, keys were often found on these bodies and key-rings. These keys seem quite relevant because sometimes these persons would bring keys or even the keys given to them during an identification session, they could try them out to open a vehicle or a flat. And it would be confirmed in this way whether this set of keys belonged to their husband, son and so on and so forth. This is the sort of thing that families like to see, because this is palpable, this is tangible. This is solid evidence, and it corroborates any possible identification. Sometimes these items can be highly relevant and a very convincing piece of evidence. Rock hard evidence, if you like. The last column says main identifying elements. It's self-explanatory. It can be a combination of different things, it can be just one thing, but it needs to be something that is very convincing, that is very indicative, and then this main element is derived. We like to have a combination, we like to have many things at a time. If you have more elements, needless to say, it may be easier to identify a body and the error margin is significantly reduced. It's important for one particular element to stick out, as it were, to be particularly prominent. By way of an example, this may be a document found on a body, it may be the teeth, so that any previous injury, any antemortem trauma, can provide a decisive element. For example, if somebody had an obvious injury to one of their fingers, this is something that quite a few people tend to know about, their families. There are few people with just this kind of injury, so this is rock hard. This can be used as an important thread to identify a body. So this is the sort of information that we had. This is what we used in order to have a positive ID. Something that could be seen as reliable, something that could be accepted by their families. And this is eventually how the whole process was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. You might want a glass of water after that answer. It was very complete and comprehensive. Thank you very much. And, Doctor, this chart relates to the 93 individuals who were exhumed and identified in the classical method; is that correct? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And on looking at the chart, I see that in no cases is there only one identifying feature. In every case in this chart, from what I can glean, is that there's always more than -- more than one identifying feature that would lead to a positive identification. My question for you is: Is it ever the case that you would do a positive identification on only one identifying feature, or do you always look for more?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: When trying to identify we look for several features, always. But we are also quite limited with what we actually received, what sort of remains we have on our hands. As regards Ovcara, more or less all of the bodies were complete. Therefore, based on several different features, we could ID them. Whenever we have the complete body or at least most of it, we have to come up with at least several features, including the height, the age and so on and so forth. And then we need to move on to the more solid features to reconfirm the identification. We always try to have several features, and this was a particularly good example, because the bodies were relatively well preserved, and the identification process was made easier for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And is it the case that you and the team that worked with you were responsible for the positive identification of all of these individuals that had been identified so far, the 192?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I'll put it the following way: Our team, whether we used the classical or the DNA method, we carried out our job as best we could, and we prepared the necessary identification elements, including everything needed by the family, so that they would be able to grasp what the elements are and to reach the final conclusion of who the person is. In doing so, we did everything by the book, and we prepared all the material that we had at our disposal to be presented to the family. And then the family could accept or not whether indeed that is their family member. It was a joint decision, so to say, on our part and on the part of the family, but the family gives the final "yes." And legally speaking they are responsible for the positive identification, although we did the best job we could and we tried to present it as best we could to the family. If the classical method failed, we went with the DNA method. As I've explained, when we deal with the DNA method, we come up with 99.99 per cent figures, which points to a very high statistical probability that indeed this is the person, and such results are then accepted by the family, concluding the process of identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And perhaps -- that document has been tendered already. Thank you, Doctor. If we can now turn to tab 2 of the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Smith. We know that there is a translation to follow here, but as far as I can see, there are two words which are not preliminarily translated into English. Maybe we could explore that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: It's a good idea. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Doctor, Your Honour has pointed out that the two words on the chart and I think we're referring to "da" and "ne"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE THELIN
utterances.text: No, that was sorted out before. I'm referring to -- If you look at the left-hand column, Doctor, you find the number 27 on the chart. And then you go to the right-hand column, you have two words. If you kindly enough to translate that. "Oziljci" "tetovaze," in my poor rendition. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, of course. That means scars and tattoos.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Doctor, if we could now turn to tab 2 of your folder. And this is ERN number 0600-2948 to 0600-2960. Doctor, this table was a chart that was prepared by the Office of the Prosecutor which brings together the autopsy report numbers, your 2006 identification results, and the names that appear in your 2006 list. And also on the right-hand side the names that appear in Annex A of the indictment and the year of birth. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And perhaps, if we look at the left-hand side of the table, where we see "name," the footnote perhaps number 3, you can see that it relates to the 2006 list. And also the date of birth with the footnote 2, relates to the list that you provided in the Milosevic case that we've referred to earlier of the individuals exhumed. And then also in the identification method, column number -- further along we see that also relates to your chart in the -- made in 2006. In relation to the information that's placed in this chart from the 2003 list, just -- provided by the commission for missing persons, in relation to the 2006 list, is that information accurate? Have you had a chance to have a look at this list to see that the information has been transferred correctly?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe we went through this data, and there are some discrepancies between the names here and in the other documents; namely, some spelling errors occurred when retyping. Column 3 put together in 2006 with the data after the final identification accepted by the family, and in cases where the death certificates were issued, those should be the correct, the accurate particulars.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. But I would like to take you to items or autopsy -- autopsy report numbers 65 and 66, which is on page 5 of the document. If we look at the name of the individual 65, and if we compare it with the name in the annex in the indictment you see that the surname is spelled slightly differently; the Z is different. In this case, which spelling would you say would be correct, the one in your 2006 list, or the one in the annex to the indictment, and why?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: In case number 65, I'm practically certain that the last name indeed is Zeravica, with a check, and whether there was the issue of where the list was made and whether there was a letter Z in the template, perhaps that's why we ended up with a Z. But it should have been Zeravica. As regards number 66, we have the last name appearing there with two Ls. It is a common name in our part of the world, but I've never seen it with two Ls. This is a typo. And it seems that the name mentioned in the annex is the correct one, where we have Holjevac with a single L.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can just go to one last one, which is 198, the name of the individual is in your list, is Marko Josi Jurisic; the name in the annex to the indictment is Josip -- Marko Josip Jurisic. Are you able to say which one of those spellings is correct or not?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot be fully certain, but if I try to deduce logically, the first name of Josip is a common name in Croatia, whereas Josi, I've never heard of such a name. Therefore, I presume that Josip is the correct version. But as to which one is the accurate one, I cannot be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And you've had an opportunity to study this list prior to testifying. There are also some minor spelling differences in other cases. And in those cases that we looked at which -- which spellings would you believe to be more accurate, the ones in the 2006 list, or the ones in the annex to the indictment where there is a minor difference, other than those three that we talked about?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Having gone through the two lists and compared them, it is easier for me to explain that the list which is more correct would be the one under number 3, dating back to 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And also there is a few cases where the year of birth and the date of birth have varied by one year, and in one case two years. There was four cases of that in the chart. Which -- which would you deem to be more correct, the ones in the list provided by the commission in the fourth column, or the year of birth in the annex to the indictment?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: The same reply. I cannot be certain. We would have to compare that against the death certificates, but my guess is that the fourth column is the more correct one when it says DOB(2) because that is more recent data compiled in 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And just for the assistance of Your Honours, the minor spelling differences between the 2006 list and the annex to the indictment are at numbers 4, 19, 20, 21, 34, 49, 79, 80, 110, 119, 163, 177, 188, and 191. And the slight differences in the year of birth and date of birth can be found at 147, 184, 195 and 199. Your Honours, I seek to tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 461, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Doctor, if we can now turn to tab 7, please. This is an autopsy report in relation to Ovcara victim number 9, Josip Balog, and it can be found at e-court 861. E-court page number 38. Doctor, do you see the autopsy report in your binder there? Do you have that report in front of you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, I think we've discussed this earlier, but this autopsy report was prepared by the international group of pathologists; is that correct? Or one of those pathologists?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if we look at the third page of the report, it's -- the pathologist was Bryan Mitchell and it's dated the 11th of October, 1996. You stated earlier that you received identification protocols from the international group that did the autopsies, but you didn't receive the cause of death part of their findings. In relation to this autopsy report, can you explain which part that you received in 1997 to assist you with your identification process and which part of the report you didn't receive?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: We received the entire first and the second page, and the third page up to where it says: "Trauma related to death." That part wasn't given to us. Everything before that we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And if you -- perhaps if you can take us through this report, through this example of Josip Balog and explain to us what factors here, in terms of identification features, were useful to you to perform the identification. Just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As with any other report, there is the case number as well as the autopsy date, the mean age, and the possible range. I have explained before the reason for the age range, as we couldn't establish the exact age during an autopsy. We can also determine the sex and the height, which can vary, as well as whether the person was left or right-handed. In this specific case it was unknown. After that we have clothing in detail, as it was taken off the remains, providing details for each of the items, and footwear. After that, personal effects in detail; for example, cigarettes, lighters, keys, rings, or jewellery, as well as a watch. Also occasionally medication was found on the body, as well as some other papers that can be useful with identification. In case there were any identification papers, it was stipulated in a separate -- as a separate item. And when the person was in possession of such an identification paper with the first and last name or with a telephone number, then we could make the preliminary identification using this as one of the solid elements. After that, on page 2 we have external examination. Mentioning the condition of the body. Then hair and all the details pertaining to that. As well as skin characteristics, where we have tattoos, scars, injuries and so on and so forth, anything that can be found on the skin provided it was preserved. Then we have deformity, the congenital, and the acquired ones. All fractures as well and amputations of limbs. After that there is internal examination. We look for any organs that may have been preserved. If that was the case, we described them. Then we also indicated whether there were any medical prothesis or objects, implants inserted into the body that may be important for identification. Then we have the description of the teeth; if there were none, we mentioned here that there were none. There were cases in which not a single tooth was left. After that recent injuries and evidence of hospitalisation that occurred before death in relation to injuries and perhaps hospitalisation. Then we have tracheostomy, meaning in this case the person was operated on. This was a patient who had difficulty breathing. After that we have trauma related to death that we didn't receive. In this specific case, we had multiple gunshot injuries of the mandibula, of the cervical vertebral fractures, as well as the right scapula fractures, which point to the cause of death being gunshots. Then we have the cause of death, which is the conclusion made based on the previous two items, citing here multiple gunshot wounds as the cause of death. This was so in most of the Ovcara cases. Finally we have manner of death, in this case homicide. That was the classical form used for all 200 cases. We used the same principle and we included all the data and elements we had into such documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. It's now 3.00. I just have a few questions about this document after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Okay. We will rise now for 20 minutes and we will resume at 20 past 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Doctor, you had taken us through a sample of one autopsy report in relation to Ovcara victim number 9. And you explained to us the types of components that were contained in that report from which you commenced your identifications. Attached to this report is an odontological post mortem data sheet, which you should be able to see attached and a Physicians for Human Rights Ovcara mass grave site sheet, as well as a certification of cause of death attached to the report. When you received the autopsy report or the part of it that related to the identification from the internationals in 1997, did you also receive these three documents, these type of documents attached to each of the reports, if they -- if they were there?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, we received the odontological data. Since the findings were insufficient, we had our own dental expert who examined all 200 dentitions, and he provided an additional description that we used when identifying the bodies. That's as regards the first page you mentioned. The second, I must admit I don't remember this one, because it wasn't of some particular interest for our identification. The third one, the certificate of cause of death, we didn't receive that. It was not given to us at that time, as I've explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Why was it decided to have another dental technician or someone examining the teeth over and above what was done previously by the internationals?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Out of the entire documentation we received, which was clearly defined and written down by the forensic pathologist, by the anthropologist and all the others who participated, this was the only portion, the odontological part, that was somewhat insufficient. We couldn't find our bearings in it because it lacked the essential elements for identification. We had our own expert, who was a lecturer and examiner at the time, and he was the person who specialised in forensic medicine. He provided us with a more detailed odontological finding, and we thought it to be particularly important to come up with a positive ID. We needed a more detailed report on the dentitions, because in the Ovcara cases it was quite important for identification, as we may have concluded from one of the previous tables that we looked into.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In relation to the process of identification that you've discussed throughout today, you have explained that it's been relatively involved in relation to looking at the bodies, any identifying features in terms of clothings, other articles, documents, and also in terms of looking at antemortem data and perhaps speaking to relatives and friends, et cetera. Would it be fair to say that this identification process is, in fact, an investigative process that you conducted in relation to these 200 individuals rather than a process that occurred very quickly in a short period of time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, being the short answer. As I've mentioned before, for such an identification procedure one needs to be well prepared. When we have the entire process in mind, a large portion of it is determined by good preparation. First and foremost that means putting together the list of the missing persons as well as collecting the antemortem data. We tried to establish contact with the families, with the people who may know some important details about the missing persons. They need to provide as many answers as possible. And all that is included in the preparation phase. The treatment of the body, as well as the preparations made to call the family in to identify and the overall communication with the family was very important, because it occurred in various phases of the process. These are all very important elements of the process which takes time and patience. It is the only way to carry out a quality classical-type identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And just looking at this autopsy report in relation to Josip Balog, we have that appendix to it relating to the Physicians for Human Rights. That sheet, which is 0055-970 [sic], was that sheet prepared by a group of people from Physicians for Human Rights, were they present at the exhumation and at the autopsy?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I believe what you have stated is correct. They made this list, or rather they put in the data, and I believe they were present at exhumations and autopsies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honours, I seek to tender this report in particular, but it relates to the whole 200 reports, which are identified in the 65 ter exhibit number 861. It's about 900 or so pages for the 200, and I would seek to tender all of those reports. The Prosecution have received these documents from the physicians -- a representative from the Physicians for Human Rights in 1997. In fact, we received them from Bryan Mitchell who is, in fact, I think the pathologist in this -- in this report. So we would seek to tender that exhibit, the 200 reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 462, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Doctor, in tab 7, behind the tab we have a series of photographs that relate to this individual, Mr. Josip Balog. And these photographs appear to be photographs of Mr. Balog in the grave as well as photographs taken at the post mortem. And the 65 ter number of these photographs is 867, and I would ask that -- if that could be called up on e-court, please. In the meantime, Doctor, were photographs taken of every victim at the exhumation site and of every victim when the autopsy was conducted, as far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, each person, each victim, was photographed before their bodies were pulled out of the grave. A number was attached, bodies were placed in white bags. And this was also the case each time an autopsy was performed. So there is a photograph in relation to each body.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And if we can look at the first photograph on the screen, do you see the photograph with the number 7 there?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And perhaps if we can go to the next photograph, please. Can you describe briefly what you see in that photograph?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I have to admit that the photograph is not very clear except for the number. I suppose the number is 9, although it could be an inverted 6 as well. This was obviously photographed in the grave itself. The photograph itself is quite dark, and it's difficult to discuss any details.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps if we can move to the next photo. And the next. Thank you. Doctor, look at this photograph, is this a photograph of the body of Josip Balog?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: This is a body marked as number 9, it's now been placed in a bag, and stored. Further identification indicated that this body, indeed, belonged to a person named Josip Balog.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If we could move to the next photo, please. And the next, please. And the next, thank you. If we can keep moving through, and then perhaps I'll -- I'll say if we can stop. Thanks. If we can stop there, thank you. In relation to the exhumation, firstly what can you see in this photograph, and how was the clothing treated once bodies were removed from the grave?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: The bodies, including any clothing and items, were placed in a bag marked with a number and delivered to our forensic pathology institute where autopsies were performed. All the items and clothing were taken off the bodies, the items were washed and dried, after which they were arranged like this and photographed in order to be as identifiable as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And perhaps now if we could move through the photographs from -- from this point to the end, and then I'll ask you to just to describe basically the types of photos that were taken for each of the -- each of the victims. Perhaps if we can just stop at that one, thank you. Doctor, what do you see in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: In this photograph, I can see a piece of the cranium bone. This is a gunshot wound causing a multiple fracture of the skull. After some time, the skin and soft tissue decomposes and all that remains is the bone. The bone is fragmented. This, as you see, is a mere fragment of the skull. You see where the arrow is, there is a semi-circular shape which indicates with a high degree of probability that there was a gunshot wound. This semi-circular shape or lesion indicates with a very high probability that the cause of death was a gunshot wound.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And this is 0056-1522. If we can just continue through the photographs, please. And if we can stop there. Doctor, this is an -- appears to be an identification card relating to Josip Balog. In a number of cases were identification cards found on these individuals, or similar identifying documents?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there weren't too many documents like that lying around. Some were found, such as this one, for example. This is the most valuable piece of evidence possible. Everybody keeps their ID on them. Sometimes other types of documents were found, case histories, bills issued to a certain person bearing the person's name, different types of documents. But an ID is the best thing to have, because it makes the identification process relatively simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And of the victims that had identifying documents or papers on them, did -- were those papers or documents kept by the institute in Zagreb or were they kept by the internationals?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Nearly all the documents bearing a person's name were taken to The Hague, taken delivery of by international experts, in other words. The only information we had is what you can find on the first page of our report, indicating that an ID was found, a person's name, number and address. So we knew that the piece of evidence was found, but we sometimes didn't even receive copies, let alone the original documents. It would have been useful for us to get a peek at something like this, but it wasn't available to us at the time, regrettably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: But the substance of the information was placed in the identification protocol, which was given to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I did say so, didn't I? That was on page 1, personal information. Something that we could work with and which would have given us a lead about the person's identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could continue through the photographs, please. Thank you. I think we've finished there. Doctor, just from the photographs that we've seen in relation to Ovcara victim number 9, we've seen a number of personal effects; keys, glasses, medical prescriptions and other documentation. Would it be fair to say that there was a number of leads or a number of identifying characteristics within that material to identify the right person in addition to the identification card?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's true. In this case, as we have seen, we had a number of items, clothes and other such items that were unique or peculiar in a way. Things such as sets of keys, a pair of glasses. Individual items in the sense of belonging to a particular person. The keys can be checked, can be compared to other sets of keys. This is something that families can check and accept as a positive ID. In this particular case, there were a great number of items found, as well as items of clothing found on a person, and this certainly helped us in identifying the body. Plus the ID card, obviously, which was the final proof.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. You've mentioned that the identification cards and identification papers weren't left with you at the institute for the identification process. But in relation to the clothing and personal effects that we saw, say as an example with Mr. Josip Balog, were those -- were they kept with the institute or were they taken by the internationals and taken somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: No. Everything else, clothing or other items, was left with the institute to help identify the bodies and it did, indeed, prove very helpful to our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you also had access to the -- to the individual for further identification procedures, if requested; is that correct? If required, I mean.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Each body, alongside with any items and reports, was forwarded to us. The bodies were there, there were many cases where we showed families the bodies, or they may have wanted to see a body or what remained of it. Many people asked to be there to see for themselves, to have a look and decide themselves, if their direct experience would corroborate what they could glean from any other types of evidence such as photographs and documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And in relation to the photographs of the results of the autopsy and the identification material, you didn't keep photographs of that. They were taken by the internationals when they left in 1997. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We didn't have photographs from the autopsy when injuries were defined, when bullets lodged in the bone were found. We had photographs of the teeth; there was a special photographer taking those. And this was something that we could show the families. These were preserved, and each time a body was identified, and I don't mean just the bones but everything else that the body had on it, would be shown so the families were given a chance to have a look for themselves at what we had found.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I seek to tender the photographs in relation to Ovcara victim number 9, which is 867 on the 65 ter list. And in addition to that I also seek to tender nine sets of photographs of other individuals that have been victims from Ovcara that the Prosecution has received from the Physicians for Human Rights on the 20th of October, 1997. It's just a selection of photographs rather than the whole sets for the whole 200. And those photos have 65 ter numbers of 868, 869, 870, 871, 872, 873, 874, 875, 876, and 877. And they're in the binder index, 12 to 20.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: And you want them to be one exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I think it might be easier for e-court if they're separate exhibits. And perhaps they could be assigned a number whether now or later, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Okay. Then they will be received and they will receive different numbers, but you can do that after the session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Also, whilst we're on that, Your Honour, I also would like to tender identification papers that -- or photographs of identification papers that we have received from, again, the Physicians for Human Rights who were involved in the process on the 18th of November, 1996, and there are similar identification papers to that seen in these photographs, and there are 43 individuals that were exhumed from Ovcara, and -- which including Josip Balog, they're in binder index number 9, then to 21 to 64 in the index. I can read those 65 ter numbers out or I can leave it at that in terms of identifying through the index.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, the photograph relating to 09, is that a double set, is it identical, or -- is it identical to 463, the one we have already received, or is it still another set of photographs relating to the same victim?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: 867 is of 09, and then the other nine individuals are in addition to 867, which is 09.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: 867 is the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Can the court officer manage?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There will be exhibit with a 65 ter number 867 will be Exhibit 463. And then 65 ter number 868 will be Exhibit 464. 65 ter 869, Exhibit 465. 65 ter 870, Exhibit 466. 65 ter 871, Exhibit 467. 65 ter 872, Exhibit 468. 65 ter 873, Exhibit 469. 65 ter 874, Exhibit 470. 65 ter 875, Exhibit 471. 65 ter 876, Exhibit 472. And 65 ter 877, Exhibit 473.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Okay. The court officer just tells me that she's going to give the numbers and will inform us when she has gone through all the lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Doctor, I just have a couple more questions for you. In relation to the meetings that you had with the Yugoslav commission for missing persons and as a representative of the Croatian missing persons commission in early 1990 to mid-1992, do you remember a Zoran Stankovic being a member of the Yugoslav commission or not and attending those meetings?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I do remember Zoran Stankovic being a member of the commission. I don't think he attended the first or the second meeting but then he did attend several meetings in a row. So in answer to your question, yes, he was a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was he a member of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I know. He was a captain first class at the time, as far as I remember. That was the rank that he held.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you know what position he had within the JNA, what part of the JNA he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, Zoran Stankovic was a forensic pathologist at the military medical academy. I think he was the head of forensic pathology there at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And was he present at some of those commission meetings prior to the grave being discovered in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He certainly was present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And can we assume therefore that he was present when the discussions relating to the missing people from the Vukovar Hospital were had?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As I've indicated before, this was something that was discussed at each and every meeting, starting in January 1992, and all the way up until the time the grave was discovered. One of the major subjects being discussed, normally the first one to be discussed at any meeting, was the fate of the wounded from the Vukovar Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you also know a person by the name of Miodrag Starcevic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, because I never saw this gentleman again, he was a military official in this commission. Whether he was a lieutenant-colonel or a colonel, I really don't know, but I think he was the head of the Yugoslav delegation at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And do you know which section within the JNA he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not positive, but I think he was actually an intelligence officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one last topic, if we can go to e-court, Exhibit number 256, please. It's a series of photographs. And if we could go to photograph 26, thanks. Number 26, please. If that could just be rotated 90 degrees, thank you. Oh, yes. Thank you. Doctor, looking at this photograph in front of you, do you recognise that area?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I must say it's very difficult for me to get a grip on this. I can't be certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Well, perhaps if I can assist you a little. On the left-hand side of the photograph, you see -- two-thirds of the way up you see three buildings. That is the Ovcara hangars. That is where the evacuees from the Vukovar Hospital were kept before they were -- before they were killed. In relation to that, are you able to see anywhere on this photograph the grave site where the exhumation occurred, if that helps. If you are unable to, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I was there as early as 1995 and then at the beginning of the exhumations. We passed by the hangars, I remember that. But any more than that, I can't say. This is an aerial photograph, and now I see the three hangars you pointed at, but apart from that, I can't find my bearings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I think we'll leave it at that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Strinovic. My name is Vladimir Domazet, a member of the Defence team for Mr. Mrksic, and I will cross-examine you on his behalf. Just a moment until I get the lectern, please. Mr. Strinovic, we usually tell the same thing to each witness, to pause between question and answer, particularly in such cases when we both speak the same language. I saw up until now that you were quite cautious in providing your answers, and you had the interpreters in mind; therefore, you could continue that practice and keep one eye on the screen. Dr. Strinovic, during your testimony in chief you provided some of your particulars and you've mentioned your current employment. You said that you are a professor at the medical school. Since we are interested in the time relevant to this indictment, could you perhaps tell us what your tasks or duties were at that time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: In 1991, I believe you had that in mind, I was a lecturer and an examiner at the same institute. I was also a court expert, much like today. The then head had retired, and at that time I was his -- I was only a lecturer and examiner and by now I've become deputy head. In December of 1991, I was appointed to the commission for the missing and detained persons. That is as far as the distinction between 1991 and today is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. When we talk about the commission, the member of which you began -- you became at the end of 1992, could you tell me who were the members of the commission. I'm not so much interested in the names, but in the profile of the members and who presided over the commission.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, back in 1991 and 1992 when we initiated the negotiations there was a physician in the commission, there was a lawyer as well, who was the then lecturer and examiner at the law school, there were representatives of the Red Cross, and I was there representing the forensic pathologists as a profession. And I don't know about the others. Since that time I haven't had much dealings with the commission, so I can't say any more as to the members on the Croatian side. The commission was presided over by a professor of the medical school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe you said that that commission is still in existence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Under a somewhat different name. But it is the same commission, which changed in time. At that time its main role was to negotiate, so to speak. After 1995 its focus was somewhat changed. It focused on exhumations and locating mass graves and then further processing and identification. The commission, as it is today, still maintains contacts with Serbia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, and its counter-parts there, in trying to locate those still missing on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were you the only forensic pathologist in the commission, or were there any others?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: On the Croatian side, I was the only one, I believe. There was a forensic pathologist on the Yugoslav side, this being Dr. Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As you've explained, you were appointed by your government to monitor the operation at Ovcara. This probably had to do with your membership in the commission and because of your field of work, I believe. Perhaps both factors could have qualified you for a monitor?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so. I was a member of the commission since before that time, and that was one of the reasons why I was appointed as a monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned the task you had concerning Vukovar, and that was to establish where the people were who went missing from the Vukovar Hospital, since, according to the data you had, you presumed some of them missing and you discussed this at the commission's meetings. What was the figure you had at your disposal at that time as a commission member? And I have in mind those who went missing from the hospital.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't the one to come up with the figures. Those are the figures presented by the president of the commission and the Red Cross, but I remember there were several figures in circulation. 270 or 400, so it wasn't a single figure, but it varied. In any case, it pertained to the people who went missing from the Vukovar Hospital, and the figure mentioned at the time was around 400.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you said the figure varied, does that mean that it went up or down in different times and does that mean the list was expanded or reduced, why do you say the figure varied?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the list was amended. There were families coming in looking for their relatives, and the numbers increased in time. That's why the figure wasn't fixed. We received more data, we received new family inquiries, and the numbers grew. Also, some of those people would occasionally resurface, decreasing the number. That's the other reason why the figure wasn't stable.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As far as you remember, the figure varied from the initial 270 all the way up to around 400. Is my interpretation correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's how I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Either you or the commission, were you in possession of the list of the missing persons?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was a list of first and last names of the missing persons. We didn't only use the figure, but we had the actual names.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Apart from first and last names, did the list contain anything else, any other information?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember whether I actually saw that list in that form. All I can presume is that it probably contained the date of birth, address and similar, but I can't be any more precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I understand, but maybe I can refresh your memory. Apart from the first and last names, were there also information about whether those people were hospital staff or in what capacity they were at the hospital? Do you remember anything of such nature?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember today, I believe it did mention whether those people were wounded or whether they were hospital patients or hospital staff. I believe it was included, because people talked about it and it must have been mentioned somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You also testified in the Milosevic case. You provided a report there as well as some tables. In that case, you testified on some other locations; that is, on more locations than we're interested in today, but one of them still being Ovcara. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: We are first and foremost interested in the events at Ovcara, and I wanted to ask you about your appointment as monitor for the exhumations. You said you were appointed by the Croatian government. Do you remember exactly when and do you remember when it was that you came to Vukovar and Ovcara in that capacity for the first time?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR STRINOVIC
utterances.text: If you're asking me about the exact date, I really can't say. Being a member of the commission for the detained and missing persons, and since the exhumation process was supposed to have been monitored, it was logical that out of all the members of the commission I would be appointed as the only forensic pathologist because I've dealt with the issues of identification and exhumation before. Therefore, I was elected to be monitor. As for the date, I can't say. I was at Ovcara sometime in 1995 when we toured the area, and then the second time I came there I was already a monitor and that was at the time when the exhumations began.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
